![A dorsal view of a human brain specimen.](images/ch24/gross-anatomy-dorsal-view.png){#fig-ch24-gross-anatomy-dorsal-view fig-alt="Photo of a human brain viewed from above, showing the two hemispheres."}

## Cardinal orientations

MRI volumes are described using three standard planes and axes: axial, coronal, and sagittal; anterior-posterior (A/P), left-right (L/R), and superior-inferior (S/I, also dorsal-ventral).

![Axial, coronal, and sagittal views of a structural MRI, with the cardinal anatomical directions labeled.](images/ch24/cardinal-orientations.png){#fig-ch24-cardinal-orientations fig-alt="Three MRI viewer panels showing axial, coronal, and sagittal slices with anterior, superior, and left labeled."}

## Naming conventions for sulci and gyri

It is difficult to remember all the names of the sulci and gyri. If you work in one region of the brain, you need to know its landmarks well; for other regions, some general principles suffice — for example, vision is associated with occipital and temporal cortex, reading with temporal, parietal, and frontal cortex, and hearing with temporal cortex.

![Key landmarks in and around human visual cortex: parieto-occipital sulcus, calcarine sulcus, cuneus, and lingual gyrus.](images/ch24/visual-cortex-key-names.png){#fig-ch24-visual-cortex-key-names fig-alt="Medial view of a brain specimen with the parieto-occipital sulcus, calcarine sulcus, cuneus, and lingual gyrus labeled."}

Neurologists and psychologists commonly use a structure-function naming scheme — frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes — which is a loose approximation with imprecise functional associations.

![The four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital, with the central sulcus, precentral gyrus, and lateral (Sylvian) fissure labeled.](images/ch24/lobes-structural-definition.png){#fig-ch24-lobes-structural-definition fig-alt="Lateral view of a brain with the four lobes colored and labeled."}

### Lateral view

![Lateral view landmarks: precentral and postcentral gyrus, central sulcus, parieto-occipital sulcus, lateral (Sylvian) fissure, and preoccipital notch.](images/ch24/lateral-view-labels.png){#fig-ch24-lateral-view-labels fig-alt="Lateral view of a brain with major gyri, sulci, and the Sylvian fissure labeled."}

![Detailed labels of gyri and sulci on the lateral surface: superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyrus; pre- and postcentral gyrus; supramarginal and angular gyrus; superior, middle, and inferior temporal gyrus; lateral occipital gyri.](images/ch24/gyri-sulci-labels.png){#fig-ch24-gyri-sulci-labels fig-alt="Detailed lateral view of the brain with many gyri and sulci labeled by name."}

### Insula

![The insula lies buried within the lateral (Sylvian) fissure, between the frontal and temporal lobes.](images/ch24/insula.png){#fig-ch24-insula fig-alt="Lateral brain view with a boxed region over the Sylvian fissure, and a second panel showing the insula exposed by retracting the frontal and temporal opercula."}

![Medial view showing the corpus callosum, anterior commissure, diencephalon, brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla), cerebellum, and spinal cord.](images/ch24/medial-view-brainstem-labels.png){#fig-ch24-medial-view-brainstem-labels fig-alt="Medial view of the brain with the corpus callosum, brainstem subdivisions, cerebellum, and spinal cord labeled."}

![A closer view of the diencephalon and midbrain: hypothalamus, fornix, dorsal thalamus, pineal gland, superior and inferior colliculus, anterior commissure, optic chiasm, pituitary gland, mammillary body, cerebral aqueduct, and fourth ventricle.](images/ch24/diencephalon-midbrain-labels.png){#fig-ch24-diencephalon-midbrain-labels fig-alt="Close-up medial view of the diencephalon and midbrain with many structures labeled."}
